# Bark: NIP-07 Nostr Signer with NIP-46 Remote Signing

> Bark is a browser extension (Chromium, Firefox, and Safari) that implements
> NIP-07 (`window.nostr`) and bridges all signing to a remote NIP-46 signer.
> No keys in the browser.

## What Bark does

Bark provides the standard `window.nostr` interface that Nostr web apps expect:
- `window.nostr.getPublicKey()`: returns the active public key
- `window.nostr.getRelays()`: returns the active signer's relay list
- `window.nostr.signEvent(event)`: signs a Nostr event
- `window.nostr.nip04.encrypt(pubkey, plaintext)` / `.decrypt(pubkey, ciphertext)`: legacy NIP-04 encryption
- `window.nostr.nip44.encrypt(pubkey, plaintext)` / `.decrypt(pubkey, ciphertext)`: NIP-44 encryption

All signing is delegated to a remote NIP-46 bunker. Bark itself stores zero key
material.

## Works with any NIP-46 bunker

Paste a `bunker://` URI from nsecBunker, Amber, nsec.app, or any NIP-46-compliant
signer, or pair by scanning a `nostrconnect://` QR code. Standard signing works
out of the box.

## Heartwood persona extensions

When connected to a Heartwood signer, Bark exposes persona management under
`window.nostr.heartwood`, which forwards to Heartwood-specific NIP-46 RPC
methods via `BunkerSigner.sendRequest()`:

- `window.nostr.heartwood.listIdentities()`: calls `heartwood_list_identities`,
  returns all derived identities on the device
- `window.nostr.heartwood.derivePersona(name, index)`: calls
  `heartwood_derive_persona`, derives a new identity from the device mnemonic
- `window.nostr.heartwood.switch(target)`: calls `heartwood_switch` with a
  target (npub, persona name, purpose, or `"master"`); current Heartwood
  signers select identity per bunker connection instead, so this is kept for
  older Heartwood builds and third-party callers

## Architecture

Eight source files in `src/`, one runtime dependency (nostr-tools):

- `provider.js`: injects `window.nostr` into pages
- `content-script.js`: bridges page and extension messaging
- `background.js`: NIP-46 connection, request routing, policy checks
- `policy.js`: pure allow/ask/deny policy engine
- `popup.js` / `popup.html`: UI for connections, personas, relay health, policy
- `approve.js` / `approve.html`: the approval surface for ask-policy requests

## How Bark differs from other NIP-07 signers

- No local keys: unlike nos2x or Alby, keys never exist in the browser
- Any NIP-46 bunker: unlike Remote NIP-07 (Amber only), works with any bunker
- Persona derivation: unique to Bark and Heartwood, no other extension does this
- Privacy mode: can hide `window.nostr` from every site except an explicit allowlist
- Focused: one job, expose standard NIP-07 while signing through NIP-46

## Policy system

Bark evaluates a layered allow/ask/deny policy before forwarding each request.
Rules are checked in priority order, first match wins:

1. Site-specific kind rule (e.g. kind 0 at a trusted site)
2. Site-specific method deny (a blocked site stays blocked)
3. Global kind rule
4. Site-specific method default
5. Global method default
6. Fallback: deny

Default policy: `getPublicKey`, `getRelays`, `signEvent`, `nip04.encrypt`,
`nip04.decrypt`, `nip44.encrypt`, `nip44.decrypt`, and every `heartwood_*`
method are `ask`. Event kinds 0 (profile metadata), 3 (contact list), and
10002 (relay list) remain protected even after a site is trusted unless
explicitly overridden.

When a request triggers `ask`, Bark opens an approval popup. The user can
allow once, trust the site, or deny. Bark also shows a temporary notice in
the requesting page; its Review in Bark action foregrounds an approval window
that the browser opened out of sight. The policy is configurable per method,
per event kind, and per origin.

## Multi-instance support

Bark supports multiple simultaneous bunker connections. Each instance stores:
- A unique ID and user-chosen name
- Bunker URI (connection string, not a private key)
- Client secret (NIP-46 auth credential, not a signing key)
- The active signing pubkey (which may differ from the bunker's master key if
  persona switching is in use)
- Whether the connected signer is a Heartwood device

Users switch between instances in the popup. All data lives in
`chrome.storage.local`. Legacy single-connection storage is automatically
migrated on first load.
